comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
Escape 2 in this epic's Context was corrected after the fact: the original text said role-scoped simulate-principal-policy PROVED the planned IAM grant would have failed in production. It did not — that simulator conclusion was itself wrong, and only a real from-instance call settled it (the Converse API authorizes against bedrock:InvokeModel, not bedrock:Converse; see ticket 9249 for the full reversal).

This makes the example STRONGER, not weaker, and the epic text now reflects it: the investigation used two successive instruments, and NEITHER could observe the failure mode it was being used to rule out — a bedrock:* identity because it could not fail at all, and a policy simulator because it answers what the policy language permits for a NAMED action rather than which action the service CHECKS.

Design consequence for this epic's child story: the measurement-provenance contract should capture not only WHERE and UNDER WHAT PRIVILEGE a measurement was taken, but what KIND of instrument produced it (simulation / static analysis / live call) — because a simulation and a live call are not interchangeable evidence for an authorization claim, and the current attestation shape cannot tell them apart.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
A FIFTH escape shape — and it REFINES this epic's framing, so recording it here rather than as a separate finding.

This epic currently draws the line as: the gates caught things when "the ground truth lived in the repo, where the reviewer's read/grep tools could REACH it", and missed things whose measurement lived in the world. A case found this run shows that line is drawn in the wrong place.

THE CASE (full detail on eb6e-f43a-e86b-443a): S8's plan asserts "The model stays Claude; only the route changes", with a Scope of one env var (the bot service's REBAR_LLM_MODEL). That assertion is FALSE, and provably so from the repo alone: resolve_model routes step > workflow > config; code-review.yaml declares no per-step model so all four passes take cfg.model; review_kernel/verify.py:269 only downgrades Pass-2/Pass-4 to sonnet when model == "claude-opus-4-8" EXACTLY, so any bedrock: id disables the downgrade; and config.py:333-341 maps bare "claude" -> anthropic, so plan-review.yaml:62-65's bare model_ladder keeps calling Anthropic after the cutover. One env var cannot express the four-pass model mapping the cutover needs.

WHY IT MATTERS TO THIS EPIC: the ground truth here is 100% in-repo and fully reachable — no AWS call, no billing, no world. It was still invisible, because it is FOUR HOPS across FOUR files that the plan never cites. The reviewer pins the ticket's own material plus its direct dependencies' material; S8 cites voter.py:69 and infra paths and nothing on the model-resolution path. So the binding constraint is not REACHABILITY, it is CITATION: the gate reads what the plan points at, and a plan's most dangerous claims are exactly the ones it does not point at, because the author did not know they needed checking.

That is a sharper and more tractable target than "world-grounded evidence". A claim like "only the route changes" is an assertion about the system's OWN runtime behaviour, and today nothing asks the plan to show its work for it. It reads to a reviewer as SCOPE DISCIPLINE — a virtue — which is why it survives; the plan is rewarded for the narrow Scope that is itself the defect.

CANDIDATE STORY for this epic, distinct from the existing three children: a criterion (advisory-first per ADR-0054, consistent with this epic's design) that fires when a plan asserts unchanged behaviour across a substrate/route/provider swap WITHOUT citing the resolution path that would make it true. Detection sketch: a swap-shaped plan (provider/route/endpoint/model change) whose Scope touches only configuration, and whose citations include no file on the path that consumes that configuration. The remedy it asks for is cheap and mechanical — cite the resolution chain, or state the assertion as an open question.

NOTE ON TIMING, so this is not misread: S8 has NOT been plan-reviewed yet (plan_review_phase: planning, empty keyring). The gate did not miss this — it has not run. This is a PREDICTED escape, argued from what the gate reads rather than from an observed failure, and it should be labelled as such until the review actually runs on S8. If the review DOES surface the routing gap unprompted, that is direct evidence against this candidate story and it should be dropped.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
CONFIRMED, with measurements — this upgrades the earlier "predicted escape" comment on this epic from
a prediction to an observed instance, and the prediction's own disconfirming test did NOT fire.

Earlier I argued this epic's framing was drawn in the wrong place: not REACHABILITY of ground truth, but
CITATION of it. I logged a candidate story and an explicit way to disprove it ("if the review DOES surface
the routing gap unprompted, drop the candidate"). It did not. Here is the evidence.

THE ESCAPE: the per-pass model collapse — one env var cannot express four passes; `verify.py:269` returns
the verifier default ONLY when the model equals the framework default, so ANY non-default model (every
Bedrock id) silently disables the Pass-2/Pass-4 downgrade; and Pass-1's ladder is BARE `claude-*` names
that infer provider `anthropic`, so a "Bedrock" run can still send its finders to direct Anthropic. Now
tracked as 3768-789c-11ed-48be, which blocks BOTH remaining stories of epic 061c.

MEASUREMENT 1 — the gate never ran on the two tickets where the defect lives. Counting REVIEW_RESULT
events in the store: epic 061c has 2 (it WAS reviewed, and signed). Story eb6e (S8, the cutover) has
ZERO. Story 0d76 (S6, the parity bar) has ZERO. Plan-review runs at CLAIM time, and neither story has
been claimed. So for those two, "the review missed it" is FALSE — no review has ever run. That distinction
matters for this epic's design: a criterion that only fires at claim time cannot protect a decomposition.

MEASUREMENT 2 — nothing pointed at the defect. I checked whether ANY ticket in the tree (the epic, S5
343b, S6 0d76, S8 eb6e) names `resolve_verifier_model`, `verify.py`, or `model_ladder` anywhere in its
description. The answer is 0 of 3 for EVERY one of them. The reviewer reads the material the plan cites;
no plan cited the three files where the collapse lives. Ground truth was 100% in-repo, needed no AWS call,
and was a three-hop trace — and was still invisible.

MEASUREMENT 3 — the epic-level review passed and signed. So a reviewed, signed plan sat directly above a
defect that made two of its stories unimplementable as written. An epic plan describes the GOAL; the
defect lived in the mechanism, which no story's Scope named.

WHAT ACTUALLY TRIGGERED THE DISCOVERY: an operator stating a desired end state ("Pass-1 should use opus,
Pass-2/Pass-4 sonnet"), which forced the question IS THIS EXPRESSIBLE. No gate asks that. Gates ask
whether a plan is well-formed, grounded and testable. S8's "The model stays Claude; only the route
changes" is well-formed, grounded-sounding, and reads as commendable SCOPE DISCIPLINE — the camouflage is
that the defect looks like a virtue.

THE SAME SHAPE RECURRED TWICE MORE IN THE SAME RUN, which is why I think it is a class and not an anecdote:
- Story 343b was reviewed, PASSED, implemented under held-out TDD with mutation checks, and still shipped a
  field that never reaches a production payload — because every test fed the persist step a hand-built
  verdict, and the uncited assembly path (`orchestrator.finalize_verdict`) was never exercised. Found only
  by an [operator-attested] criterion demanding a REAL run.
- 3768's own plan-review then found a THIRD inverted gate (`completion.py:332`) that my plan had not cited
  — again, the uncited path was the broken one.

REFINED CANDIDATE CRITERION for this epic: advisory-first, fires when a plan asserts UNCHANGED BEHAVIOUR
across a substrate/route/provider swap while citing NO file on the path that consumes the swapped
configuration. Detection sketch: a swap-shaped plan (provider/route/endpoint/model change) whose Scope
touches only configuration, and whose citations include no consumer of that configuration. The remedy it
asks for is cheap: cite the resolution chain, or restate the assertion as an open question. S8 would have
tripped it on "only the route changes" with a Scope of one env var.

SECOND, NARROWER CANDIDATE suggested by measurement 1: the decomposition itself is unguarded. Stories are
reviewed only when claimed, so a tree can be decomposed, signed at the epic level, and sit for a whole
implementation run with story-level defects unexamined. Worth considering whether an epic-level review
should be able to require that its children's mechanisms are cited somewhere, even before they are claimed.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body: E1 (f161) plan-review reached PASS/signed on round 4, then was revised once more to honour this epic's own recorded design decision: the provenance contract now carries a FOURTH required field, instrument=<live-call|simulation|static-analysis>, alongside environment/principal/privilege_posture. Rationale (surfaced by the G7 criterion, verified against this epic's COMMENT event): privilege_posture cannot distinguish a simulator from a live call - both can honestly declare production-equivalent - so escape 2b (simulate-principal-policy returning a confident WRONG authorization conclusion that only a real from-instance call refuted) would have stayed invisible in the record. This epic has exactly one child, so no sibling could deliver it. Also added a deterministic trigger to the AGENT-tier criterion so an ~85x-cost criterion routes only on plans carrying [operator-attested], not on every plan.

compiled_state.description:
# Gate blindness to world-grounded evidence: force measurement provenance into the record

## Context / Problem

A `/rebar-implement` run of epic `061c-ecd1-8967-4a76` landed five changes through every gate. **The gates
performed to their design envelope.** Plan-review blocked infeasible mechanics (a tenacity-transport claim that
cannot wrap boto3; an `isinstance` against a botocore-dependent class; a live canary path that would have made
billable AWS calls on every CI run). The completion-verifier twice refused a close whose stated criteria had no
test. Full-suite pre-flight caught cross-module regressions `tests/unit` missed.

Every one of those catches shares a property: **the ground truth lived in the repo**, where the reviewer's
read/grep tools could reach it.

Four escapes got through, and they are one defect wearing different clothes — **a green signal whose
measurement could not have observed the failure it claims to rule out**:

1. **Wrong environment.** Bedrock caching and model-availability measurements were taken in account
   `579718921998` / `us-east-2` and recorded as settled fact; the project runs in `896586841071` / `us-east-1`
   (named by the Terraform backend `rebar-tfstate-896586841071`). No gate compares a claim's observation
   context against the project's environment. A human caught it by asking "is that this project's account?"
2. **Instruments that cannot observe the failure — twice, in the same investigation.** This escape is the
   epic's sharpest example precisely because the *first correction was also wrong*.

   **2a.** Live `bedrock:Converse` calls validated a *scoped* IAM grant while running under an identity
   holding `bedrock:*`. Evidence generated under broader privilege than production is structurally unable to
   fail, so its success carries **zero information**.

   **2b.** The prescribed remedy — `aws iam simulate-principal-policy` against the role — then produced a
   confident, recorded, and **wrong** conclusion: that `bedrock:Converse` was the action to grant. The
   simulator answered exactly the question asked ("would this policy permit the action *named*
   `bedrock:Converse`?", legitimately no, since that action genuinely exists) but **not** the question that
   mattered ("which action does the Converse API actually *check*?"). Only a real call FROM the instance
   revealed the truth — `AccessDeniedException ... not authorized to perform: bedrock:InvokeModel` — meaning
   the ORIGINAL plan was right and the "fix" broke it, on a role feeding `eb6e-f43a-e86b-443a`, a cutover
   with no fallback.

   The pair is the lesson: a wildcard identity could not fail, and a simulator could not fail *for the reason
   that mattered*. **Evidence is only as good as its ability to have come out the other way for the reason
   you care about** — and swapping one instrument for a more rigorous-sounding one does not establish that.
3. **Tests that cannot fail** — the code-side form of the same defect: a contrast case whose discriminating
   conjunct was never exercised, and an oracle asserting on an object where production passes a string.
   **Both WERE caught** (mutation testing; the LLM reviewer) precisely because they are repo-checkable. That
   contrast is the evidence for this epic's thesis.
4. **Confidence outrunning method**: "verified by reading" was a hand-picked grep that missed a dependency;
   "18/18 green" was reported while typecheck was red.

## Why 1 and 2 are structural, not a calibration miss

`verified_at_sha` pins the code world completely and the outside world not at all. Plan-review runs **before**
the evidence exists, so it cannot audit a measurement not yet taken; the completion-verifier accepts
`[operator-attested]` evidence **on trust by design** (ADR-0043). One gate cannot audit it, the other is
designed not to. The in-flight T5c rewrite pushes grounding toward current code and IaC state but still cannot
observe a live cloud account — nothing in the current design can, and nothing should try.

## Approach

Do **not** make a gate observe the world. Force the measurement's context into the record as text, then let the
existing repo-grounded machinery find contradictions in it. Detail lives in the child story; the shape is:

1. Extend the attested-evidence contract with measurement-provenance fields — environment, principal, and
   privilege posture relative to production.
2. Enforce their **presence** deterministically, zero LLM, mirroring
   `src/rebar/llm/plan_review/det_operator_attested.py` (DET-first doctrine).
3. Let an LLM criterion judge the *declaration* against repo facts — once provenance is text, "plan attests
   account X, IaC names account Y" becomes a **repo-checkable contradiction**, which is exactly what the
   gate's strongest criteria already do well.
4. Land the generalized rule as an **advisory** criterion per ADR-0054; corpus replay decides promotion.

## Explicitly rejected

- **Making the completion-verifier re-run world measurements.** Expensive, flaky, recursive — the verifier's
  own credentials carry the same privilege-masking problem, so it would validate using the instrument under
  suspicion.
- **Escape 4 as gate scope.** Reported-green-while-red is *reporting discipline*, already covered by the
  orchestration rule that agents report gate output faithfully rather than narrating success. Filing it as a
  gate gap would be mis-attribution.
- **Wording changes alone.** The contract was followed and still failed; emphasis is not the defect. This is
  the same lesson as epic `9109-2ad9-2477-4cf6` (Serena tool-choice), which is why that epic's structural
  framing is the model here rather than its subject matter.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] an `[operator-attested]` criterion lacking measurement provenance is flagged by a DETERMINISTIC check
      (no LLM), and the wrong-account escape is reproduced as a regression fixture from the real
      `579718921998` vs `896586841071` case
- [ ] the new criterion ships **advisory** (ADR-0054) and rides the `.rebar/` project overlay, leaving the
      shipped default criteria set unchanged for other rebar clients
- [ ] an ADR records the amended evidence contract, citing ADR-0043 as the shape it changes
- [ ] the completion-verifier is NOT made to re-run world measurements — the rejected alternative stays
      rejected, and a test or grep demonstrates it
